_about: Mars overlay, deep-merged over data/text.json (arrays replace). Owners: campaign and screens (M4) everything here except survey, instruments and drill (milestones and survey, M5). Integration (M6) wires the sol, night and storm strings into the HUD; they may use the {placeholders} of missionVars() in src/ui/tutorialText.ts. Every real fact cites its source (historySources, campaign.sources).

partText._about: Mars wording for the shared parts (data/parts.json), by part id; numbers stay the Moon's. Mars-only parts carry their wording in data/parts.json itself. Matches the Mars rules: no driving at night without lights, map-wide night cold, solar income by day only and less in a dust storm, soft ground only in Seitah's sand ripples.

wheels-solid.description: Cheap and heavy. Lower grip in sand ripples.

power-fixed-panel.description: A flat panel. Solar income by day, most with the Sun high. Nothing at night, less in a dust storm.

power-solar-mast.description: Twice the fixed panel's solar income. Nothing at night, less in a dust storm. Light, expensive and bulky.

lights-none.description: Saves cost, mass, and space. The rover cannot drive at night.

lights-led.description: Lets the rover keep driving at night, at a high battery cost.

heater-none.description: Saves cost, mass, and space. Without another source of heat the rover freezes in its first night.

heater-rhu.description: Steady heat from decaying isotopes. Lets the rover survive the night cold.

instrument-drill.name: Rock drill
instrument-drill.description: Drills rock cores. Heavier and bulkier than the camera.

slots._note: Names of the support slots Mars offers (data/mars/parts.json supportSlots), merged into the shared slot names.

support._note: Support hardware on the desk (Mars M5): an instrument whose support part is missing is refused with a reason. {support}: the support part's name below; {part}: the instrument.
support.missing: {part} needs the {support}. Choose it, or take the instrument out of the bay.

landing.heading: Landing: Jezero crater
landing.briefing: The lander has touched down on the floor of Jezero crater on Mars. The crater is about 45 km wide and held a lake, fed by a river that built a delta, about 3.5 billion years ago. The rover is deploying.

ticket.briefing: REL secures a spot for the rover on the next commercial launch to Mars. The lander will set it down on the floor of Jezero crater.

nightBudget._note: The spec sheet's night budget line (Mars M15): one night's energy for this build, asleep and parked awake with the lights on, the electric heater's share of each, and an RTG's income over the night. Numbers from data (rules/energy.ts nightBudget). Shown once power, lights and heater are chosen.
nightBudget.label: Night energy ({seconds} s)

design.overTopTier: Exceeds the Heavy ticket limits. The rover cannot launch.
speedInfo: The mission compresses {sols} sols on Mars into {minutes} minutes. Driving is compressed too: rovers in this game drive {compression} times faster than the real speeds their parts are modeled on.

On Apollo 15 in 1971, the crew reported that about 6 to 7 km/h was the most comfortable driving speed for the Lunar Roving Vehicle. Its top speed was of the order of 9 to 13 km/h, depending on slope, roughness, and soil.
Robotic rovers drive far slower. NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars have a top speed of about 4 cm/s (0.15 km/h) on flat ground.

campaign.carryOver: Balance carried over from the Moon: {balance}.
campaign.passMark: After this mission the balance must stay at or above {minimum}, the pass mark for Titan.
campaign.sameParts: Mars has its own parts: the Moon's, without the two instruments that have no work on this mission, plus new power sources, a larger battery, an electric heater, grouser wheels, an arm, a mast and four Mars instruments. Launches to Mars have their own ticket tiers, with a Heavy tier.
campaign.ticketNote: Launches to Mars have their own ticket tiers: the Moon's three, and a Heavy tier for rovers up to 100 kg.
campaign.perseverance: NASA's Perseverance rover landed in Jezero crater on February 18, 2021. Its landing site, Octavia E. Butler Landing, is about {distance} km {direction} of the lander.
newOnMars: Sols: the mission lasts {sols} sols. Each sol is {daySeconds} s of daylight followed by {nightSeconds} s of night.
Night: keep the lights on to continue driving, at a high battery cost and with no solar income, or power down with P and sleep until dawn. Without lights the rover cannot drive at night.
Cold: every night the rover cools, everywhere on the map. A heater slows freezing.
Dust storm: an orbital weather report forecasts the storm about {stormLeadSols} sol ahead. During the storm, solar income falls to about {stormSolarPercent}%.
campaign.sources: Sources: NASA JPL, Mars 2020 Landing Press Kit: Landing Site (www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mars_2020/landing/mission/landing_site/); NASA, Welcome to 'Octavia E. Butler Landing' (www.nasa.gov/image-article/welcome-octavia-e-butler-landing/).

mission.briefing: Ten sols at Jezero crater. The Sun sets every sol: lights on to keep driving, or sleep until dawn.
mission.controls: W A S D or arrow keys to drive. Space to brake. P to power down (sleep) or power up.

hud.endedSurvived: The rover completed ten sols at Jezero crater.
hud.lasted: The rover operated for {days} of {total} sols.

warnings.lowEnergy: Battery low. Recharge in sunlight, or power down with P.
warnings.cold: Night cold. The rover is freezing.

sol.lasted: The rover operated for {sols} of {total} sols.

night.sunset: Sunset. Lights on to keep driving, or sleep until dawn.
night.dawn: Dawn. The solar panel is charging again.
night.sleeping: Asleep until dawn. The rover wakes by itself.
night.noLights: No lights: the rover cannot drive at night. Power down with P to sleep until dawn.
night.lightsOn: Lights on. The battery is draining.

storm.forecast: Orbital weather report: a regional dust storm reaches the site in about {stormLeadSols} sol. Solar income will fall to about {stormSolarPercent}%.
storm.started: Dust storm. Solar income is down to about {stormSolarPercent}%.
storm.cleared: The dust storm has cleared. Full solar income has returned.
storm.credit: The weather report is modeled on the daily global weather maps from the MARCI camera on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Source: NASA Science, Mars Color Imager (MARCI) for Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (science.nasa.gov/resource/mars-color-imager-marci-for-mars-reconnaissance-orbiter).

debrief.failedRound: The balance is below the pass mark for the next mission, Titan ({minimum}). The round must be restarted. Balance, research points and records return to their values at the start of the Mars round.
debrief.passedRound: The balance meets the pass mark for the next mission, Titan ({minimum}). The Mars round is complete.

history.survived: NASA's Opportunity rover was designed for a 90-sol mission on Mars and kept working for more than 14 years, from its landing in January 2004 to its last signal on June 10, 2018.
history.froze: NASA's Spirit rover, embedded in soft soil since 2009, could not tilt itself toward the low winter Sun; without power for its survival heaters it likely became colder inside than in any earlier winter. Its last communication was on March 22, 2010.

historySources.survived: NASA, NASA's Record-Setting Opportunity Rover Mission on Mars Comes to End (www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-record-setting-opportunity-rover-mission-on-mars-comes-to-end)
historySources.froze: NASA JPL, NASA Concludes Attempts to Contact Mars Rover Spirit (www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-concludes-attempts-to-contact-mars-rover-spirit/)

comingSoon.heading: Titan: coming soon
comingSoon.body: The Mars mission is complete. The Titan mission is in development. Research points and the balance are banked for it.

design.title: Mission 2: Mars
body: The campaign continues on Mars, on the floor of Jezero crater. The balance carried over from the Moon is {balance}.

Mars has its own parts. The Moon's carry over, without the laser retroreflector and the seismometer station, which have no work to do on this mission. New are a radioisotope generator and deployable solar arrays, a larger battery, an electric heater, grouser wheels, a robotic arm and a mast for instruments that need them, and four Mars instruments. Launches to Mars have their own ticket tiers: {tiers}.

After the mission, the balance must stay at or above the pass mark for Titan ({nextMinimum}), or the Mars round is restarted. A restart returns the balance, research points and records to their values at the start of the Mars round.

design.title: Designing for the night
body: Each sol on Mars ends with a night. The solar panel earns nothing at night and less while the Sun is low, so the battery must carry the rover through every night.
With lights the rover can keep driving at night, but the lights drain the battery. Without lights it cannot drive at night and can only sleep until dawn.
Nights are cold everywhere on the map. A heater slows freezing; without one, the rover freezes quickly at night.

design.title: Dust storm
body: One regional dust storm reaches the site during the mission. For about {stormSols} sols, solar income falls to about {stormSolarPercent}%.
A larger battery, or a rover that can sleep through the storm, keeps the mission going.

drive.title: Sols on Mars
body: W A S D or arrow keys to drive. Space to brake. P to power down or power up.

The mission lasts {minutes} minutes, which represent {sols} sols. Each sol is {daySeconds} s of daylight followed by {nightSeconds} s of night; the night is time-lapsed faster than the day. There is no clock: time is read from the Sun.
The solar panel earns most with the Sun high, less in the morning and evening, and nothing at night.

drive.title: Night: lights on or sleep
body: At sunset a notice reads: "{sunsetNotice}"
Lights on: the rover keeps driving and can still earn milestones, but the lights drain the battery and the panel earns nothing.

Sleep: power down with P. The battery drains slowly, the rover cannot drive or earn milestones, and it wakes by itself at dawn. A rover that stays awake without driving still uses some power, so sleep is the cheapest choice.
A rover without lights cannot drive at night. If the battery runs out at night, the mission ends.

drive.title: Night cold and damage
body: Every night the cold meter rises, everywhere on the map, and it falls again by day. When it is full, the rover freezes. A heater slows freezing, and nights are milder during the dust storm.
Hard impacts and ground steeper than {maxSlope}° damage the rover, as on the Moon. Sand ripples are soft ground where the wheels can dig in.

drive.title: Dust storm forecast
body: An orbital weather report forecasts the dust storm about {stormLeadSols} sol before it arrives.
For about {stormSols} sols, solar income falls to about {stormSolarPercent}%. Charge the battery before it arrives, drive less, or sleep through it.

drive.title: Instruments and map

instrument.camera: Camera: {key} (or its button) takes a photograph. Photographs count toward milestones at the delta-front viewpoint, and away from the lander with the setting Sun low in the frame: face west as the Sun goes down.
instrument.drill: Drill: stop the rover, then press {key} (or its button) to drill a core sample. Samples count at up to three sites, each at least {sampleSpacing} m from the lander and from each other.

body: Each instrument in the payload bay has a number key, 1 to {bayMax} in bay order, and a button beside the meters.
The engineering notebook records what the mission teaches about the rover. Open it with N or the Notebook button; the mission pauses while it is open, and Escape closes it.

The map starts zoomed in on the lander and widens as the rover explores. It shows only ground within {revealRadius} m of where the rover has been, and sites appear once the rover finds them. Arrows at the edge of the map point toward the orbital survey leads from the landing briefing.

terrainFallback: Terrain: USGS Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation HiRISE and CTX elevation models of Jezero crater.
credits.imageryFallback: USGS Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation HiRISE orthomosaic of Jezero crater.

survey._owner: M5. Lead ids match data/mars/tuning.json survey.leads. Directions and distances are computed, so the text names none.
survey._sources: Delta: Fassett and Head, GRL 32 (2005), doi.org/10.1029/2005GL023456. Seitah: NASA JPL, "NASA's Perseverance Rover Begins Its First Science Campaign on Mars" (jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-perseverance-rover-begins-its-first-science-campaign-on-mars/). HiRISE scale: uahirise.org/TRA_000823_1720; usgs.gov/news/mars-2020-mission-be-guided-usgs-astrogeology-maps.
survey.intro: Orbital data from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter show three areas of interest near the landing site. Directions and distances are measured from the lander and are approximate: orbital maps locate areas, not exact sites. The rover's own survey locates each site; until then, an arrow at the edge of the map points toward each area.

delta.name: Delta front
delta.source: Orbital images show the fan of an ancient river delta, first described as a delta built into a crater lake in 2005. Its front is a cliff where the layers are exposed.

seitah.name: Séítah
seitah.source: HiRISE images show ridged rock with sand ripples between the ridges; the ripples are soft ground. Séítah means "amidst the sand" in the Navajo language.

rocks.name: Boulder field
rocks.source: HiRISE images, at about 25 cm per pixel, show a rough patch of boulders on the crater floor.

survey._siteNames: Display names for the terrain.json site names, which the pipeline keeps ASCII (shown in the Located notice).

instrumentText._note: Mars's own instruments (Mars M4, behavior built in Mars step 4a) and the X-ray's slope refusal. Real facts use the safe wording of the Mars engineering plan's Real anchors (ranges, "signals consistent with"); each cites its source. Placeholders: rules/types.ts InstrumentText.

xray.slope: {name}: the ground here is too steep for the arm ({slope}°). The arm reads on ground up to {max}°.

weather.controls: {key} to switch the weather mast on or off ({standby} energy/s while on). It reads pressure and dust in the air.
weather.notCarried: This rover carries no weather mast.
weather.forecast: Weather mast: the pressure and dust readings point to a regional dust storm reaching the site in about {sols} sols, before the orbital report. Solar income will fall to about {stormSolarPercent}%.
weather.log: Weather mast: recorded pressure and dust for {seconds} s.
weather.logStorm: It forecast the dust storm before the orbital report.
weather.fact: NASA's Perseverance rover carries MEDA, a set of weather sensors that measures pressure, temperature, wind, humidity and dust in the air at Jezero crater.
weather.source: Rodriguez-Manfredi et al. (2021), The Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer, MEDA, Space Science Reviews 217:48, doi:10.1007/s11214-021-00816-9

radar.controls: {key} to switch the ground-penetrating radar on or off ({standby} energy/s while on). It images the buried layers along the drive.
radar.notCarried: This rover carries no ground-penetrating radar.
radar.log: Ground-penetrating radar: longest unbroken profile {meters} m. Ground profiled: {layers}.
radar.fact: NASA's Perseverance rover carries RIMFAX, a ground-penetrating radar. Along the rover's drives it imaged rock layers beneath the floor of Jezero crater, some of them inclined rather than flat.
radar.source: Hamran et al. (2022), Science Advances, doi:10.1126/sciadv.abp8564; UCLA news release, August 25, 2022 (www.college.ucla.edu/2022/08/25/mars-underground-images-from-perseverance-rover)

laser.controls: {key} for a laser reading of a boulder or cliff ahead (stop first; {energy} energy each).
laser.notCarried: This rover carries no laser spectrometer.
laser.holding: Laser reading. The rover holds still.
laser.noTarget: {name}: nothing to read ahead. Face a boulder or the delta cliff within {reach} m.
laser.target: Laser target: {target}, {distance} m. Press {key} to read it.
laser.resultCliff: Laser reading of the delta cliff: fine layers of sedimentary rock.
laser.fact: The laser of SuperCam, on NASA's Perseverance rover, analyzes rocks up to about 7 m away.

organics.controls: {key} for an organics reading beside a boulder (stop first; {energy} energy over a long reading).
organics.notCarried: This rover carries no organics spectrometer.
organics.holding: Organics reading. The rover holds still.
organics.target: Boulder within reach. Stop and press {key} for an organics reading.
organics.result: Organics reading complete. The rock's spectrum is stored for scientists on Earth.
organics.stopped: {name}: reading stopped. The battery could not pay for the rest of it.
organics.log: Organics spectrometer: finished readings: {count}. Spectra stored.
organics.fact: SHERLOC, on NASA's Perseverance rover, detected signals consistent with organic molecules in rocks on the floor of Jezero crater. It identified no specific compounds, and sources other than life are not ruled out.
organics.source: Sharma et al. (2023), Diverse organic-mineral associations in Jezero crater, Mars, Nature 619:724-732, doi:10.1038/s41586-023-06143-z

instruments._owner: M5: Mars overrides of the shared instrument notices, plus the sunset notices (rules/marsTypes.ts MarsInstrumentText).
instruments.photoNoZone: Photograph added to the album. Milestones count only at viewpoints, or with the setting Sun low in view.
instruments.sunsetHint: The setting Sun is low in view. Press {key} to take a photograph.
instruments.sunsetTooHigh: The Sun is in view but still high. The sunset photo counts once it is within {max}° of the horizon.
instruments.sunsetTooClose: The setting Sun is in view, but the rover is only {distance} m from the lander. The sunset photo counts at least {min} m away.
